title: The Tragic Death of Natalie Wood
summary: Stuff You Should Know episode on the 1981 death of actress Natalie Wood, who drowned after disappearing from the yacht Splendor off Catalina Island over Thanksgiving weekend 1981. The hosts cover Wood's early career and family background, her marriages to Robert Wagner, the yacht weekend with Christopher Walken and captain Dennis Davern, the initial accidental-drowning finding and high blood alcohol level, conflicting accounts from witnesses and Davern, the 2011 reopening of the case, the 2012 change in cause of death, and the family divide. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about gratitude and ingratitude lists.

entities.name: Little Sister: My Investigation into the Mysterious Death of Natalie Wood

segments.title: Opening banter and Natalie Wood introduction
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, comparing a look-alike and introducing Natalie Wood's famous films such as Miracle on 34th Street, Rebel Without a Cause, West Side Story and Brainstorm.

segments.title: Wood's childhood and early Hollywood abuse allegations
segments.summary: Background on Natalie Wood and sister Lana Wood, born to Russian immigrants in San Francisco. Finstad's biography describes a controlling mother and alleged sexual abuse by Kirk Douglas at age sixteen and a liaison with Frank Sinatra arranged by her mother.

segments.title: Marriages to Robert Wagner and career decline
segments.summary: Wood's first marriage to Robert Wagner ended in 1961 amid rumors of an affair with Warren Beatty, which the hosts say is disputed. She remarried Richard Gregson, then Wagner again in 1972. Her career tailed off as she aged.

segments.title: Setting up the November 1981 story
segments.summary: Hosts set the scene for November 1981, when Wood was 43 and Wagner 51, and preview the mystery.

segments.title: Thanksgiving 1981 yacht trip and drowning discovery
segments.summary: Wood, Wagner, Christopher Walken and yacht captain Dennis Davern took the yacht Splendor to Catalina Island. They dined at Doug's Harbor Reef and drank heavily. Wood's body was found the next morning about a mile from the anchored yacht, and the dinghy Valiant was found washed up with oars locked and ignition off.

segments.title: Initial autopsy and accidental drowning finding
segments.summary: Medical examiner Thomas Noguchi reported a blood alcohol level of 0.14 and bruises consistent with a fall overboard. The hosts explain what that BAC level means. The accidental drowning ruling became the official line.

segments.title: Psychological autopsy and Noguchi's demotion
segments.summary: Noguchi commissioned a psychological autopsy, did not release it, and mentioned Wood's drinking at a press conference. This drew anger from Hollywood, including Frank Sinatra and the Screen Actors Guild, and he was demoted.

segments.title: Shifting accounts and Wagner's explanation
segments.summary: Wagner's accounts of the night changed over time, including a 1986 story about a political argument with Walken and a 2008 autobiography saying the fight was about Wood's career. Wagner said Wood went to the cabin to do her hair. Walken supported Wagner's version in a 1997 Playboy interview. Wood had said she was afraid of dark water.

segments.title: Witness accounts and threatening note
segments.summary: Witnesses on the nearby boat Capricorn reportedly heard a woman calling for help and a man's slurred voice. Marilyn Wayne reported receiving a threatening note three days after the death. The hosts note that police did not interview Wayne and Pain.

segments.title: Dennis Davern's changed story and the night's fight
segments.summary: Davern later said he had lied to police, described jealousy over Walken, and said Wagner shouted during a fight and told him to get off his boat. He recounted hearing a scuffle and then silence, which the hosts say does not match Wayne's account.

segments.title: Davern's account of the missing dinghy and being kept in Wagner's house
segments.summary: Davern said Wagner checked the cabin, found Wood missing, and told him not to turn on lights or engine. Davern said he was kept at Wagner's Beverly Hills house for weeks, which he later described as like a hostage situation.

segments.title: 2011 reopening of the investigation
segments.summary: In November 2011 the LA Sheriff's Department reopened the case. Wagner and Walken were not treated as suspects. The statute of limitations had run out for lesser charges. Investigators received a new account of Walken saying Wagner pushed Wood overboard.

segments.title: 2012 cause-of-death change and new evidence
segments.summary: In summer 2012 the cause of death was changed to undetermined drowning and other factors. Photographer Vidal Herrera described head wounds and Michael Franco described friction burns and bruises inconsistent with a fall, and said Chief Examiner Noguchi told him some things were better left unsaid.

segments.title: Family divide and unsolved status
segments.summary: Lana Wood pressed for reinvestigation and suspects Wagner of a drunken rage, while Wagner's daughters defended him. Lana's 2021 memoir Little Sister reports Wagner's explanation after the funeral. The case is now considered an open unsolved case.

segments.title: Hosts' closing reflections on the case
segments.summary: Hosts discuss whether the truth will ever come out, noting only Davern, Walken and Wagner know what happened, and remark on the human tragedy.

segments.title: Listener mail: ingratitude lists
segments.summary: Listener Gareth writes about ingratitude lists, a way to vent about problems instead of listing gratitude. Hosts read it aloud and name it best recent email.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give the email address for listener mail, followed by the show credit.
